title: Deponent and semi-deponent verbs

objectives.can: Recognise a deponent verb: passive in form, active in meaning.

explanation.summary: A deponent verb has passive endings but an active meaning: *loquor* looks like a passive and means 'I speak'. Deponents are among the commonest verbs in Latin and the Vulgate is full of them, so the first skill is to stop reading a -tur ending as 'is being done' without checking the verb.

sections.heading: Passive in form, active in meaning
body: The earlier lessons taught that -r, -ris, -tur, -mur, -mini and -ntur make the passive. A set of verbs has only these endings and no active forms at all. *loquor* is 'I speak', *loquitur* is 'he speaks' and *loquuntur* is 'they speak'. Such a verb is called deponent, from a Latin word meaning 'to put aside', because grammarians said it had put aside its active forms and its passive meaning.

The meaning is active: the subject does the action, and the verb can take an object. *sequitur me* is 'he follows me', not 'he is followed by me'. The corpus follows the meaning and tags deponent forms as Voice=Act, though the endings are passive. When you parse them, give the voice as active.

sections.heading: Which verbs are deponent
body: A deponent is deponent in every form, and a dictionary shows it by giving a headword in -or with no active form. There is no rule of meaning that decides it, so each verb is learned as it is met. Many describe speech (*loquor*), movement (*ingredior*, *egredior*, *proficiscor*), feeling (*misereor*), or being affected (*patior*, *nascor*, *morior*).
Deponents occur in all four conjugations, and their endings are those of the ordinary passive of the same conjugation.

sections.heading: Infinitives and participles of deponents
body: A deponent has the passive infinitive in form, but it is active in sense: *loqui*, *sequi*, *pati*, *nasci* mean 'to speak', 'to follow', 'to suffer', 'to be born'. This is why a form in -i is not always a passive infinitive.

The present participle is the same as for any verb, and active (*loquentem*, 'speaking'). The perfect participle is the surprise: it is passive in form and active in sense, and so it gives a deponent the active perfect that Latin otherwise lacks. *locutus* is 'having spoken', and with a form of *sum* it makes the perfect: *locutus est* is 'he spoke'.

sections.heading: Semi-deponents
body: A few verbs are active in the present, imperfect and future, and take passive forms only in the perfect system. They are called semi-deponents. *gaudeo* is the usual example: *gaudet* is an ordinary active form, 'he rejoices', but its perfect is made from a perfect participle and *sum*, as for a deponent, and means 'he rejoiced'. *audeo*, *soleo* and *confido* are semi-deponent in the same way.
In the library the present forms of these verbs are tagged active like those of any verb. Their perfect forms are too uncertain to be offered in exercises.

sections.heading: Reading a passive-looking form
body: When you meet a verb ending in -tur or -ntur, ask what the headword is. If the headword ends in -or and has no active form, the verb is deponent and the sense is active. If it ends in -o, the form is a true passive. Both kinds can stand in the same verse: *salvabitur* is a passive ('he will be saved') and *ingredietur* is a deponent ('he will go in'), yet both end in -tur.

misunderstandings: A deponent is not a passive that the author has made active. The passive endings are the only ones the verb has; you cannot make an active of *loquor* by changing the ending.
Deponent perfect participles are not passive: *locutus est* means 'he spoke', not 'he was spoken to'. When such a participle has an object, the object is in the accusative, as with any active verb.

Not every -or headword in a text is deponent. A true passive of an ordinary verb has the same ending, and the dictionary form is the only certain guide. The exercises here draw only on verbs that are deponent in every form.

deeper.heading: Why Latin has deponents
body: Many deponents describe actions in which the subject is affected by what it does: speaking, following, being born, dying. Some linguists link the passive endings of these verbs to an older middle voice, which marked that the subject had a stake in the action. Latin lost the middle voice as a separate category but kept some of its verbs with passive endings. This is one explanation among others, and it is not needed for reading.

examples.analysis: *sequitur* ends in -tur, but *sequor* is a deponent: it means 'follows' and takes *me* as its object. The participle *locutus* is perfect, passive in form and active in sense; with *est* it gives 'spoke'. Both are tagged active.

quoted.english: I am the door. By me, if any man enter in, he shall be saved: and he shall go in, and go out, and shall find pastures.

examples.analysis: A true passive and two deponents with the same ending. *salvabitur* is the future passive of *salvo*: 'he will be saved'. *ingredietur* and *egredietur* are future deponents: 'he will go in', 'he will go out'. Only the headword tells them apart.
